statement: Assume GCH. Let $F$ send each [regular cardinal](c:is-regular) $\kappa$ to a cardinal, with $F$ nondecreasing and the [cofinality](c:cofinality) of $F(\kappa)$ greater than $\kappa$. Then a cofinality-preserving [forcing](c:forcing) extension satisfies ZFC and $2^\kappa=F(\kappa)$ for every regular $\kappa$.

hypotheses.text: The ground model satisfies the generalized continuum hypothesis.
The class function $F$ on the [regular cardinals](c:is-regular) is nondecreasing: $\kappa<\lambda$ gives $F(\kappa)\le F(\lambda)$.
The [cofinality](c:cofinality) of $F(\kappa)$ is greater than $\kappa$ for every regular $\kappa$.

conclusion: Some forcing extension that preserves cofinalities is a model of ZFC in which $2^\kappa=F(\kappa)$ for all regular $\kappa$.

proofs.name: Easton class forcing
proofs.slogan: Add the prescribed number of subsets to each regular cardinal by a class product, then count subsets in the extension.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline of Easton's class forcing and rests on the cited paper for the chain-condition and closure lemmas. The theorem controls the power function at regular cardinals only, so it says nothing about singular cardinals beyond what [cardinal arithmetic](c:cardinal-arithmetic) forces.

roles.why: GCH in the ground model gives the chain condition of the head and the size bounds for names.
Monotonicity keeps the head poset $P_{\le\kappa}$ of size at most $F(\kappa)$.
A [cofinality](c:cofinality) above $\kappa$ makes $F(\kappa)^\kappa=F(\kappa)$ under GCH.

steps.slogan: Define the Easton product of Cohen posets with Easton support.
steps.detail: For each regular $\kappa$, the poset $P_\kappa$ adds $F(\kappa)$ subsets of $\kappa$ by conditions of size less than $\kappa$. The class [forcing](c:forcing) $P$ is the product of all $P_\kappa$, where a condition has support of size less than $\gamma$ below each regular $\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Split the forcing at $\kappa$ into a small head and a closed tail.
steps.detail: Write $P=P_{\le\kappa}\times P_{>\kappa}$. Under GCH the Delta-system lemma gives the $\kappa^+$ chain condition for $P_{\le\kappa}$. The Easton support makes $P_{>\kappa}$ $\kappa^+$-closed, so it adds no new subsets of $\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Show that the extension keeps all cardinals and cofinalities.
steps.detail: The chain condition of the head keeps the cardinals above $\kappa$, and the closure of the tail keeps the cardinals up to $\kappa^+$. The usual factor argument at each regular cardinal then shows that no cardinal collapses and every [cofinality](c:cofinality) stays the same.

steps.slogan: Count the new subsets of $\kappa$ to get $2^\kappa\ge F(\kappa)$.
steps.detail: A density argument shows that the $F(\kappa)$ generic subsets of $\kappa$ added by $P_\kappa$ are pairwise distinct. So the [power set](c:power-set) of $\kappa$ has size at least $F(\kappa)$ in the extension.

steps.slogan: Count nice names for subsets of $\kappa$ to get $2^\kappa\le F(\kappa)$.
steps.detail: Under GCH the head $P_{\le\kappa}$ has size at most $F(\kappa)$ because $F$ is nondecreasing. Nice names for subsets of $\kappa$ number at most $F(\kappa)^\kappa$, and $F(\kappa)^\kappa=F(\kappa)$ because the cofinality of $F(\kappa)$ exceeds $\kappa$. The tail adds no new subsets of $\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds and check that ZFC holds in the extension.
steps.detail: The bounds give $2^\kappa=F(\kappa)$ for every regular $\kappa$, and preserved cofinalities keep the regular cardinals of the ground model regular. Easton checks in the cited paper that the class extension satisfies ZFC.

concepts.c:is-regular: The theorem prescribes the power function exactly at regular cardinals.
concepts.c:forcing: Forcing builds the model in which the power function takes the prescribed values.
concepts.c:cardinal-arithmetic: Cardinal arithmetic at singular cardinals lies outside the prescribed values.
concepts.c:power-set: The value $2^\kappa$ is the size of the power set of $\kappa$.

source.ref: W. B. Easton, Powers of regular cardinals, Annals of Mathematical Logic 1 (1970), 139-178
source.note: The steps follow Easton's class forcing; a textbook treatment is T. Jech, Set Theory, 3rd millennium edition, Springer 2003, Theorem 15.18.

statement: Take a [commutative diagram](c:commutative-diagram) of [abelian groups](c:abelian-group) with rows $A\xrightarrow{f}B\xrightarrow{g}C\xrightarrow{h}D$ and $A'\xrightarrow{f'}B'\xrightarrow{g'}C'\xrightarrow{h'}D'$, [exact](c:exact-sequence) at the middle terms, and vertical maps $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$. If $\alpha$ is [surjective](c:surjection) and $\beta,\delta$ are [injective](c:injection), then $\gamma$ is injective. If $\alpha,\gamma$ are surjective and $\delta$ is injective, then $\beta$ is surjective.

hypotheses.text: The two rows are connected by vertical maps $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ so that the [diagram commutes](c:commutative-diagram).
Both rows are [exact](c:exact-sequence) at the two middle terms: $\ker g=\operatorname{im}f$, $\ker h=\operatorname{im}g$, and the same for the primed row.
For the first claim, $\alpha$ is [surjective](c:surjection) and $\beta$ and $\delta$ are [injective](c:injection).
For the second claim, $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ are surjective and $\delta$ is injective.

conclusion: Under the first set of conditions $\gamma$ is injective, and under the second set $\beta$ is surjective.

proofs.name: Diagram chase
proofs.slogan: Chase an element through the two rows, using exactness to move sideways and the outer maps to correct the choice.
proofs.scope: Abelian groups, by element chasing; any abelian category follows from the Freyd-Mitchell embedding. The first claim uses exactness at $B$, $C$ and $B'$, and the second uses exactness at $C$, $B'$ and $C'$.

roles.why: Commutativity moves each element from the top row to the bottom row.
[Exactness](c:exact-sequence) turns a vanishing image into a preimage in the row.
Injectivity of $\delta$ and $\beta$ and surjectivity of $\alpha$ drive the first chase.
Surjectivity of $\gamma$ and $\alpha$ and injectivity of $\delta$ drive the second chase.

steps.slogan: Send an element of $\ker\gamma$ down to $D$ and use injectivity of $\delta$.
steps.detail: Let $c\in C$ with $\gamma(c)=0$. Commutativity gives $\delta(h(c))=h'(\gamma(c))=0$. Because $\delta$ is [injective](c:injection), $h(c)=0$.

steps.slogan: Lift $c$ to $B$ by exactness at $C$ and push it into $B'$.
steps.detail: Exactness at $C$ gives $b\in B$ with $g(b)=c$. Then $g'(\beta(b))=\gamma(g(b))=0$, so exactness at $B'$ gives $a'\in A'$ with $\beta(b)=f'(a')$.

steps.slogan: Pull $a'$ back along $\alpha$ and use injectivity of $\beta$ to show $c=0$.
steps.detail: Because $\alpha$ is [surjective](c:surjection), $a'=\alpha(a)$ for some $a\in A$. Then $\beta(f(a))=f'(\alpha(a))=\beta(b)$, so $b=f(a)$ since $\beta$ is injective. Hence $c=g(f(a))=0$ by exactness at $B$.

steps.slogan: Choose $c\in C$ with $\gamma(c)=g'(b')$ and show that $h(c)=0$.
steps.detail: Let $b'\in B'$. Since $\gamma$ is surjective, some $c\in C$ has $\gamma(c)=g'(b')$. Then $\delta(h(c))=h'(g'(b'))=0$ by exactness at $C'$, so $h(c)=0$ because $\delta$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Lift $c$ to $b\in B$ and compare $\beta(b)$ with $b'$.
steps.detail: Exactness at $C$ gives $b\in B$ with $g(b)=c$. Then $g'(b'-\beta(b))=g'(b')-\gamma(c)=0$, so exactness at $B'$ gives $a'\in A'$ with $b'-\beta(b)=f'(a')$.

steps.slogan: Correct $b$ by an element of $f(A)$ to reach $b'$.
steps.detail: Write $a'=\alpha(a)$, which is possible because $\alpha$ is surjective. Then $\beta(b+f(a))=\beta(b)+f'(\alpha(a))=\beta(b)+f'(a')=b'$. So $\beta$ is surjective.

steps.slogan: Read both claims off the two chases.
steps.detail: The first chase shows $\ker\gamma=0$ under the first set of conditions. The second chase shows that every $b'$ lies in the image of $\beta$ under the second set.

concepts.c:commutative-diagram: Commutativity lets the chase pass from the top row to the bottom row.
concepts.c:abelian-group: Elements and subtraction make the chase possible in abelian groups.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness converts a zero image into a preimage along the row.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjective outer maps supply the preimages that correct the choices.
concepts.c:injection: Injective outer maps force an element to be zero or equal to another.

source.note: The standard diagram chase, as in the textbook proofs of the five lemma (for example Mac Lane, Homology, Chapter I); the four lemma is the half of that chase that uses four columns.

statement: Let $\lambda$ be a [partition](c:integer-partition) of $n$ with irreducible [character](c:character-of-a-representation) $\chi_\lambda$ of the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_n$, and let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be vectors over a field of characteristic $0$. The [tensor](c:tensor) $\sum_\sigma\chi_\lambda(\sigma)v_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma(n)}$ is nonzero if and only if the vectors split into [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset) sets whose sizes are the parts of the conjugate partition $\lambda'$.

hypotheses.text: The function $\chi_\lambda$ is the irreducible [character](c:character-of-a-representation) of $S_n$ that belongs to the [partition](c:integer-partition) $\lambda$ of $n$.
The vectors $v_1,\dots,v_n$ lie in one vector space over a field of characteristic $0$.

conclusion: The symmetrized tensor is zero exactly when the vectors have no split into independent sets of sizes $\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots$.

proofs.name: Young symmetrizer reduction
proofs.slogan: Reduce the vanishing of the symmetrized tensor to Young symmetrizers, whose column part forces independent columns.
proofs.scope: The outline follows Gamas (1988) and the short proof of Berget (2009); the hard direction, that independent columns survive row symmetrization, is quoted from them. Over a field of characteristic $0$ the group algebra of $S_n$ is semisimple.

roles.why: The character $\chi_\lambda$ fixes the central [idempotent](c:idempotent) and the shape $\lambda$ of the tableau.
The vectors fill the columns of the tableau and must be independent there.

steps.slogan: Write the symmetrized tensor with the central idempotent of $\chi_\lambda$.
steps.detail: Let $t=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ and let $e_\lambda$ be the central [idempotent](c:idempotent) of $\chi_\lambda$ in the group algebra. The symmetrized tensor equals $\frac{n!}{\chi_\lambda(1)}e_\lambda t$. So it is nonzero if and only if the module generated by $t$ has a $\lambda$-isotypic part.

steps.slogan: Replace the idempotent by a Young symmetrizer applied to all rearrangements.
steps.detail: For a [Young tableau](c:young-tableau) of shape $\lambda$, let $c_\lambda=a_\lambda b_\lambda$ be the product of the row symmetrizer and the column antisymmetrizer. The module generated by $t$ has a $\lambda$-part if and only if $c_\lambda(\sigma t)\neq0$ for some $\sigma\in S_n$. Here $\sigma t$ is $t$ with the vectors rearranged.

steps.slogan: Show that a nonzero Young symmetrizer forces independent columns.
steps.detail: If $c_\lambda s\ne0$ then $b_\lambda s\ne0$. The antisymmetrization of a column is nonzero only when the column vectors are [linearly independent](c:linearly-independent-subset). So the columns give a split into independent sets of sizes $\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots$.

steps.slogan: Show that independent columns survive the row symmetrization for a good arrangement.
steps.detail: If the vectors split into independent sets of these sizes, then some arrangement of them in the tableau has $a_\lambda b_\lambda s\ne0$. Gamas (1988) proves this by a combinatorial analysis, and Berget (2009) gives a short proof; the argument is not repeated here.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the criterion.
steps.detail: By the first two steps the tensor is nonzero if and only if some arrangement has $c_\lambda s\ne0$. The third step gives the split into independent sets from such an arrangement, and the fourth step gives such an arrangement from a split.

concepts.c:integer-partition: The partition $\lambda$ sets the shape of the tableau and its column lengths.
concepts.c:character-of-a-representation: The irreducible character picks the isotypic part that the symmetrization projects onto.
concepts.c:symmetric-group: The symmetric group permutes the tensor factors and carries the character.
concepts.c:tensor: The symmetrized tensor is the object whose vanishing the theorem decides.
concepts.c:linearly-independent-subset: Independent columns are exactly what makes the column antisymmetrization nonzero.
concepts.c:idempotent: The central idempotent projects the tensor onto the $\lambda$-isotypic part.
concepts.c:young-tableau: The tableau of shape $\lambda$ places the vectors in rows and columns.

source.ref: C. Gamas, Conditions for a symmetrized decomposable tensor to be zero, Linear Algebra and its Applications 108 (1988), 83-119
source.note: A short proof is A. Berget, A short proof of Gamas's theorem, Linear Algebra and its Applications 430 (2009), 791-794, doi 10.1016/j.laa.2008.09.027.

statement: For every $n\ge1$ there is a number $f(n)$ such that every [finite subgroup](c:finite-group) $G$ of the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})$ has an [abelian normal subgroup](c:abelian-normal-subgroup) of [index](c:index) at most $f(n)$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
The group $G$ is a subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})$ for some $n\ge1$.

conclusion: The group $G$ has an abelian normal subgroup $A$ with $[G:A]\le f(n)$, and $f(n)$ depends on $n$ only.

proofs.name: Commutators near the identity
proofs.slogan: Make the group unitary, split on whether elements near the identity are scalar, and induct on the dimension.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge1$ by induction on $n$; the case $n=1$ is trivial because $\mathrm{GL}(1,\mathbb{C})$ is abelian. The bound $f(n)$ is not explicit.

roles.why: Finiteness gives an invariant inner product and a positive distance of every non-identity element from $I$.
The embedding in $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{C})$ gives matrices, norms and the dimension for the induction.

steps.slogan: Make $G$ unitary by averaging an inner product over $G$.
steps.detail: Average the standard [inner product](c:inner-product-space) over the finite group $G$ to get a $G$-invariant one. In an orthonormal basis for it, $G$ lies in the [unitary group](c:unitary-group) $U(n)$, and indices and abelian normal subgroups do not change.

steps.slogan: Bound the distance of a commutator from the identity.
steps.detail: For unitary $A,B$ in the [operator norm](c:operator-norm), $[A,B]-I=(AB-BA)A^{-1}B^{-1}$ and $AB-BA=(A-I)(B-I)-(B-I)(A-I)$. Hence $\|[A,B]-I\|\le2\|A-I\|\,\|B-I\|$.

steps.slogan: Split on whether the elements near the identity are all scalar.
steps.detail: Put $\varepsilon=\min(1/4,\sin(\pi/n))$ and $S=\{g\in G:\|g-I\|<\varepsilon\}$. Conjugation keeps $S$ fixed, so $H=\langle S\rangle$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$. Either every element of $S$ is scalar, or $S$ has a non-scalar element.

steps.slogan: Descend by commutators to a non-scalar element of the center of $H$.
steps.detail: Start from a non-scalar $s\in S$. If $s$ fails to commute with some $y\in S$, then $[s,y]\in S$ is non-scalar with $\|[s,y]-I\|<\tfrac12\|s-I\|$: step 2 gives the bound, and a scalar commutator $c$ has $c^n=1$ and $|c-1|<\varepsilon$, which forces $c=1$. The finite group stops this at a non-scalar $z\in S$ that commutes with $S$, so $z$ is central in $H$.

steps.slogan: In the scalar case, bound the index of the scalar subgroup by a covering number.
steps.detail: Cover the compact group $U(n)$ by $N=N(n)$ balls of radius $\varepsilon/4$. If $g,g'\in G$ lie in one ball, then $g^{-1}g'\in S$ is scalar. So $G\cap\{\text{scalars}\}$ is an abelian normal subgroup of index at most $N$.

steps.slogan: In the other case, split the space by the center of $H$ and apply induction.
steps.detail: The center $Z$ of $H$ is an abelian normal subgroup of $G$ with a non-scalar element, so $\mathbb{C}^n$ splits into $m$ joint eigenspaces of $Z$ with $2\le m\le n$, and $G$ permutes them. The kernel $K$ of this action has index at most $n!$ and acts on eigenspaces of dimension less than $n$. Induction and a core argument give an abelian normal subgroup of $G$ with index at most $n!\,M^{n\cdot n!}$, where $M=\max_{k<n}f(k)$.

steps.slogan: Take the larger of the two bounds as $f(n)$.
steps.detail: In the scalar case the index is at most $N(n)$, and in the other case it is at most $n!\,M^{n\cdot n!}$. Put $f(n)$ equal to the larger bound; it depends on $n$ only.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness gives the invariant inner product and the discreteness used in the descent.
concepts.c:general-linear-group: The group sits inside the general linear group, where norms and dimension are available.
concepts.c:abelian-normal-subgroup: The theorem produces this subgroup; a core in $K$ gives it for $G$.
concepts.c:index: The bounded index is the content of the theorem.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: An invariant inner product turns the group into a group of isometries.
concepts.c:unitary-group: Unitary matrices have norm one, so the commutator estimate holds.
concepts.c:operator-norm: The operator norm measures how far a matrix lies from the identity.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality of $H$ lets the center of $H$ be normal in $G$.

source.note: The Bieberbach-Frobenius route of 1911: unitary averaging, commutators near the identity, induction on the dimension. The constants are chosen here for a self-contained write-up.

statement: For every [Boolean function](c:boolean-function) $f\colon\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$ of one variable and every $x\in\{0,1\}$, $f(f(f(x)))=f(x)$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f$ sends $\{0,1\}$ to $\{0,1\}$, so it is a [Boolean function](c:boolean-function) of one variable.
The argument $x$ is an element of $\{0,1\}$.

proofs.name: Four cases
proofs.slogan: A map of the two-element set is determined by two values, so check the four maps one by one.
proofs.scope: All four maps $\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$ and both values of $x$. Nothing else is needed, because a function on two points is fixed by its two values.

roles.why: The map has only four possible forms, so a case split covers it completely.
The identity is checked at both points, so the cases hold for every $x$.

steps.slogan: Split on the values $f(0)$ and $f(1)$.
steps.detail: Each of $f(0)$ and $f(1)$ is $0$ or $1$, so $f$ is one of four maps: two constant maps, the identity and the swap. This is the case split that mathlib makes with `cases` on `f true` and `f false`.

steps.slogan: Treat the two constant maps.
steps.detail: If $f(0)=f(1)=c$, then $f$ is a [constant function](c:constant-function) and $f(x)=c$ for every $x$. So $f(f(f(x)))=f(f(c))=f(c)=c$, and both sides of the equation equal $c$.

steps.slogan: Treat the identity and the swap through $f\circ f=\mathrm{id}$.
steps.detail: The [identity function](c:identity-function) satisfies $f\circ f=\mathrm{id}$. The swap is an [involution](c:involution): applying it twice gives $\mathrm{id}$ as well. In both cases $f(f(f(x)))=f\big((f\circ f)(x)\big)=f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the four cases for every $x$.
steps.detail: The four maps are all the maps $\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$, and each satisfies the equation at both points. So $f(f(f(x)))=f(x)$ for every $f$ and $x$.

concepts.c:boolean-function: A Boolean function of one variable has only four possible forms.
concepts.c:constant-function: A constant map returns one value, so both sides of the equation agree.
concepts.c:identity-function: The identity map fixes every point, so repeated application changes nothing.
concepts.c:involution: An involution undoes itself, so the swap satisfies $f^3=f$.

source.note: mathlib splits on f true and f false with cases and lets grind close the four cases; here the four cases are checked by hand.

statement: Let $f\colon G\to H\times I$ be a [monoid homomorphism](c:monoid-hom) whose two coordinate maps are [surjective](c:surjection). Suppose $f(g_1)$ and $f(g_2)$ have equal first coordinates if and only if they have equal second coordinates. Then the image of $f$ is the [graph](c:graph-of-a-function) of a monoid [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) $H\to I$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon G\to H\times I$ is a [monoid homomorphism](c:monoid-hom) into a [product](c:direct-product) of monoids.
Both coordinate maps $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ f$ and $\mathrm{pr}_2\circ f$ are [surjective](c:surjection).
For all $g_1,g_2\in G$, $(fg_1)_1=(fg_2)_1$ if and only if $(fg_1)_2=(fg_2)_2$.

conclusion: There is a monoid isomorphism $e\colon H\to I$ with $f(G)=\{(h,e(h)):h\in H\}$.

formal.difference: The linked declaration is the additive form; the multiplicative form MonoidHom.exists_mulEquiv_mrange_eq_mgraph states the same theorem for monoids written multiplicatively.

proofs.name: Vertical and horizontal line tests
proofs.slogan: Read the second coordinate above each first coordinate to get a homomorphism, then repeat with the coordinates swapped to get its inverse.
proofs.scope: Monoids, with no inverses needed. The two directions of the line condition give a map $H\to I$ and a map $I\to H$.

roles.why: The homomorphism property makes the constructed map multiplicative.
Surjectivity of each coordinate map makes each constructed map defined on all of $H$ or $I$.
The two implications make each map well defined and the two maps inverse.

steps.slogan: Define $e\colon H\to I$ by reading the second coordinate above each $h$.
steps.detail: For $h\in H$, surjectivity of $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ f$ gives $g$ with $(fg)_1=h$. Put $e(h)=(fg)_2$. If $g'$ has $(fg')_1=h$ too, the line condition gives $(fg')_2=(fg)_2$, so $e$ is well defined.

steps.slogan: Show that $e$ is a monoid homomorphism.
steps.detail: Choose $g,g'$ over $h,h'$. Then $f(gg')=f(g)f(g')$ has first coordinate $hh'$ and second coordinate $e(h)e(h')$, so $e(hh')=e(h)e(h')$. Also $f(1)=(1,1)$ gives $e(1)=1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the image of $f$ is the graph of $e$.
steps.detail: Each $f(g)=(h,i)$ has $i=e(h)$ by the definition of $e$. Conversely, $(h,e(h))=f(g)$ for the element $g$ chosen over $h$. So $f(G)=\{(h,e(h))\}$, the [graph](c:graph-of-a-function) of $e$.

steps.slogan: Swap the coordinates to build an inverse and conclude that $e$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: The same argument with $H$ and $I$ exchanged uses surjectivity of $\mathrm{pr}_2\circ f$ and the reverse implication. It gives a homomorphism $e'\colon I\to H$ with $f(G)=\{(e'(i),i)\}$. Since $(h,e(h))\in f(G)$, $h=e'(e(h))$, and likewise $e(e'(i))=i$, so $e$ is an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism).

concepts.c:monoid-hom: The map $f$ and the constructed map $e$ both preserve the product.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjective coordinates guarantee that every $h$ and every $i$ appears in the image.
concepts.c:graph-of-a-function: The image of $f$ is identified with the graph of $e$.
concepts.c:isomorphism: The pair of inverse homomorphisms makes $e$ an isomorphism.
concepts.c:direct-product: The target $H\times I$ carries the coordinatewise product.

source.note: mathlib builds e₁ from the vertical line test (MonoidHom.exists_mrange_eq_mgraph), builds e₂ from the swapped map, and checks that they are inverse.

statement: Let $f,g\colon X\to Y$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) at a point $x$ that is not an [isolated point](c:isolated-point) of the space $X$, and let $Y$ be a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space). Then $f=g$ on a [punctured neighbourhood](c:punctured-neighbourhood) of $x$ if and only if $f=g$ on a neighbourhood of $x$.

hypotheses.text: The maps $f$ and $g$ are [continuous](c:continuous-function) at $x$.
The target $Y$ is a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space).
The point $x$ is not an [isolated point](c:isolated-point), so every punctured neighbourhood of $x$ is nonempty.

conclusion: The maps agree on a [punctured neighbourhood](c:punctured-neighbourhood) of $x$ if and only if they agree on a neighbourhood of $x$.

proofs.name: Equal values at the point
proofs.slogan: Show that continuity and the Hausdorff property force $f(x)=g(x)$, then add the point to the punctured neighbourhood.
proofs.scope: Both implications. The reverse implication is trivial; the forward implication needs a nonempty punctured neighbourhood, which is where $x$ not isolated enters.

roles.why: Continuity makes the set where $f$ and $g$ differ a neighbourhood of $x$.
The Hausdorff property separates the two distinct values $f(x)$ and $g(x)$.
A nonisolated point makes the punctured neighbourhood nonempty, so a common point exists.

steps.slogan: Shrink a neighbourhood to a punctured one for the easy direction.
steps.detail: If $f=g$ on a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$, then $f=g$ on $U\setminus\{x\}$, which contains a [punctured neighbourhood](c:punctured-neighbourhood) of $x$.

steps.slogan: Assume $f(x)\ne g(x)$ and separate the values by disjoint open sets.
steps.detail:
The Hausdorff property gives disjoint open sets $U
i f(x)$ and $V
i g(x)$. By continuity $W=f^{-1}(U)\cap g^{-1}(V)$ is a [neighbourhood](c:neighborhood) of $x$, and $f(y)
e g(y)$ for every $y\in W$.

steps.slogan: Meet the punctured neighbourhood with $W$ to contradict equality.
steps.detail: Let $P$ be a punctured neighbourhood of $x$ on which $f=g$. Since $x$ is not isolated, $P\cap W$ contains a point $y$, and then $f(y)=g(y)$ and $f(y)\ne g(y)$. This contradiction gives $f(x)=g(x)$.

steps.slogan: Add the point $x$ to the punctured neighbourhood.
steps.detail: Now $f=g$ on $P$ and at $x$. If $P=U\setminus\{x\}$ for an open $U\ni x$, then $f=g$ on $U$, which is a neighbourhood of $x$.

steps.slogan: Join the two implications into the equivalence.
steps.detail: The step before last gives the forward implication, and the first step gives the reverse implication. Together they give the equivalence.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at $x$ turns the inequality $f(x)\ne g(x)$ into one near $x$.
concepts.c:isolated-point: A point that is not isolated has nonempty punctured neighbourhoods.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Disjoint open sets around two distinct values make the inequality stable.
concepts.c:punctured-neighbourhood: The theorem compares agreement on the punctured and the full neighbourhood.
concepts.c:neighborhood: The set $W$ is a neighbourhood on which $f$ and $g$ differ everywhere.

source.note: mathlib shows f x = g x by contradiction with continuity and the Hausdorff property (ContinuousAt.ne_iff_eventually_ne), then uses eventuallyEq_nhds_of_eventuallyEq_nhdsNE.

statement: Every [σ-complete Boolean algebra](c:sigma-complete-boolean-algebra) $B$ is isomorphic, with its countable suprema, to a quotient $\Sigma/N$, where $\Sigma$ is a [σ-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) of subsets of a set $X$ and $N$ is a [σ-ideal](c:sigma-ideal) of $\Sigma$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $B$ is a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) in which every countable subset has a supremum.

conclusion: There are a set $X$, a σ-algebra $\Sigma$ on $X$, a σ-ideal $N\subseteq\Sigma$ and an isomorphism $B\cong\Sigma/N$ that preserves countable suprema.

proofs.name: Stone space and Baire category
proofs.slogan: Represent the algebra by clopen sets on its Stone space, then divide the sets with the Baire property by the meager sets.
proofs.scope: The representation theorem, which is the core of the duality. The statement that the correspondence is a duality of categories is not proved here.

roles.why: Countable suprema exist, so the union of countably many clopen sets is close to a clopen set.

steps.slogan: Represent $B$ by clopen sets on its Stone space.
steps.detail: Let $X$ be the [Stone space](c:stone-space) of $B$. Stone's theorem gives a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra) isomorphism $b\mapsto\hat b$ from $B$ onto the clopen subsets of the compact Hausdorff space $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that a countable supremum is a union up to a nowhere dense set.
steps.detail: Let $b=\bigvee b_n$ in $B$. The set $\hat b\setminus\bigcup\hat b_n$ is closed, and a nonempty clopen $\hat c$ inside it would make $b\wedge\neg c$ a smaller upper bound of the $b_n$. So the set has empty interior and is [nowhere dense](c:nowhere-dense-set).

steps.slogan: Define $\Sigma$ as the sets that differ from a clopen set by a meager set.
steps.detail: Let $\Sigma$ be the sets $E\subseteq X$ with $E\,\triangle\,\hat b$ [meager](c:meager-set) for some $b\in B$, and let $N$ be the meager subsets of $X$. Complements stay in $\Sigma$ because $\hat b^{c}=\widehat{\neg b}$. A countable union stays in $\Sigma$ by step 2, so $\Sigma$ is a [σ-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) and $N$ is a [σ-ideal](c:sigma-ideal).

steps.slogan: Show that no nonempty clopen set is meager.
steps.detail: The compact Hausdorff space $X$ is a Baire space, so every nonempty open set is non-meager. Hence $\hat b$ meager forces $\hat b=\emptyset$, that is $b=0$.

steps.slogan: Map $b$ to the class of $\hat b$ in $\Sigma/N$ and check that this is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: The map $\varphi(b)=\hat b+N$ is a Boolean homomorphism. It is injective, since $\varphi(b)=\varphi(b')$ makes $\widehat{b\triangle b'}$ meager and step 4 gives $b=b'$. It is onto by the definition of $\Sigma$, and it sends $\bigvee b_n$ to the class of $\bigcup\hat b_n$, the supremum in $\Sigma/N$.

concepts.c:sigma-complete-boolean-algebra: Countable suprema in $B$ are what the quotient must preserve.
concepts.c:boolean-algebra: The Stone space represents the Boolean algebra by clopen sets.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The family $\Sigma$ is the σ-algebra whose quotient recovers $B$.
concepts.c:sigma-ideal: The meager sets form the σ-ideal that is divided out.
concepts.c:stone-space: The Stone space supplies the points on which the sets live.
concepts.c:nowhere-dense-set: Countable unions of clopen sets differ from a clopen set by a nowhere dense set.
concepts.c:meager-set: Meager sets are the null sets of the quotient.

source.note: The Baire-category proof on the Stone space, as in Sikorski, Boolean Algebras (Springer), for the Loomis-Sikorski representation theorem.

statement: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a map of [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) spaces with finitely generated integral homology, and $p$ a prime. If $f$ induces isomorphisms on [mod p homology](c:mod-p-homology), then $\pi_n(f)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ is an isomorphism for every $n$, so $f$ is a $p$-adic equivalence.

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).
The groups $H_n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ and $H_n(Y;\mathbb{Z})$ are finitely generated for every $n$.
The map $f$ induces isomorphisms $H_n(X;\mathbb{F}_p)\to H_n(Y;\mathbb{F}_p)$, its [mod p homology](c:mod-p-homology), for every $n$.

conclusion: For every $n$, the map $\pi_n(f)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p\colon\pi_n(X)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p\to\pi_n(Y)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ is an isomorphism.

proofs.name: Serre class of groups without p-torsion
proofs.slogan: Show that the cone of f has homology without p-torsion, then use Serre's mod-C Whitehead theorem and tensor with the p-adic integers.
proofs.scope: The implication from mod p homology to the p-adic equivalence. I take p-adic equivalence to mean that $\pi_n\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ is an isomorphism; its agreement with a weak equivalence after [p-completion](c:p-completion) is quoted, not proved.

roles.why: Serre's mod-C Whitehead theorem applies to maps of simply connected spaces.
Finite generation lets Nakayama's lemma act on the $\mathbb{Z}_p$-modules.
The vanishing of the cone's [mod p homology](c:mod-p-homology) is the input of the argument.

steps.slogan: Define the class of abelian groups whose elements have order prime to $p$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal C$ be the class of abelian groups in which every element has finite order prime to $p$. It is closed under subgroups, quotients and extensions, and it is an ideal: $A\in\mathcal C$ gives $A\otimes B$ and $\operatorname{Tor}(A,B)$ in $\mathcal C$. It also meets Serre's acyclicity axiom, and $A\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p=0$ for $A\in\mathcal C$ because integers prime to $p$ are units of $\mathbb{Z}_p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the mapping cone of $f$ has homology in the class.
steps.detail: The cone $C$ has $\tilde H_n(C;\mathbb{F}_p)=0$ by the exact sequence of $f$, and $H_n(C)$ is finitely generated. The universal coefficient theorem gives $H_n(C)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p=0$, so Nakayama's lemma gives $\tilde H_n(C)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p=0$. Hence $\tilde H_n(C)$ is a finite group of order prime to $p$, so it lies in $\mathcal C$.

steps.slogan: Pass from homology to homotopy with Serre's mod-C Whitehead theorem.
steps.detail: The exact sequence of the cone shows that the kernel and cokernel of $H_n(f)$ lie in $\mathcal C$ for every $n$. For maps of simply connected spaces, the mod-$\mathcal C$ form of the Whitehead theorem gives the same for the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group): $\ker\pi_n(f)$ and $\operatorname{coker}\pi_n(f)$ lie in $\mathcal C$.

steps.slogan: Tensor the homotopy statement with $\mathbb{Z}_p$ to remove the class.
steps.detail: The kernel and cokernel of $\pi_n(f)$ vanish after $\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$, because groups in $\mathcal C$ do. Since $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$, tensoring commutes with kernels and cokernels. So $\pi_n(f)\otimes\mathbb{Z}_p$ is an isomorphism.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Serre's mod-C Whitehead theorem needs simply connected spaces.
concepts.c:mod-p-homology: The hypothesis is an isomorphism on this homology, which makes the cone acyclic mod p.
concepts.c:p-completion: The p-adic equivalence is read through homotopy groups tensored with the p-adic integers.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: The conclusion concerns homotopy groups, which the class argument transfers from homology.

source.note: The mod-C route of J.-P. Serre, Groupes d'homotopie et classes de groupes abéliens, Annals of Mathematics 58 (1953), 258-294; see also Spanier, Algebraic Topology, Chapter 9.

statement: Let three [circles](c:circle) in a plane have pairwise different radii, none inside another. For each pair, the two external common [tangent lines](c:tangent-line) meet in a point. The three points so obtained are [collinear](c:collinear-points).

hypotheses.text: Three [circles](c:circle) in a plane have pairwise different radii, and none of them lies inside another.

conclusion: The meeting points $E_{12},E_{13},E_{23}$ of the external tangent lines of the three pairs are [collinear](c:collinear-points).

proofs.name: Menelaus' theorem
proofs.slogan: Compute the ratio in which each meeting point divides the segment of centers, and see that the three ratios multiply to minus one.
proofs.scope: Different radii make the external tangents of each pair meet; equal radii give parallel tangents, a case that this proof does not treat. The proof covers centers that are not collinear, and collinear centers.

roles.why: Non-nested circles have external tangents, and different radii make them meet.

steps.slogan: Locate the meeting point as the center of the positive homothety.
steps.detail: An external tangent meets the line $c_ic_j$ at a point $E$, because $r_i\ne r_j$. Similar right triangles, and the fact that $c_i,c_j$ lie on one side of the tangent, give $c_i-E=\frac{r_i}{r_j}(c_j-E)$. So $E=E_{ij}=\frac{r_ic_j-r_jc_i}{r_i-r_j}$ for both tangents; it is the center of the [homothety](c:homothety) that maps circle $i$ to circle $j$.

steps.slogan: Compute the signed ratio in which $E_{ij}$ divides the segment $c_ic_j$.
steps.detail: From the formula, $E_{ij}-c_i=\frac{r_i(c_j-c_i)}{r_i-r_j}$ and $c_j-E_{ij}=-\frac{r_j(c_j-c_i)}{r_i-r_j}$. So $E_{ij}$ differs from both centers, and the signed ratio $\overline{c_iE_{ij}}/\overline{E_{ij}c_j}$ equals $-r_i/r_j$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the three signed ratios and apply the converse of Menelaus' theorem.
steps.detail: If $c_1,c_2,c_3$ are not collinear, the ratios along the sides of triangle $c_1c_2c_3$ multiply to $(-r_1/r_2)(-r_2/r_3)(-r_3/r_1)=-1$. By the converse of Menelaus' theorem, $E_{12}$, $E_{23}$ and $E_{13}$ are [collinear](c:collinear-points).

steps.slogan: Treat collinear centers by the line of centers.
steps.detail: If $c_1,c_2,c_3$ lie on one line, each $E_{ij}$ lies on the line $c_ic_j$, which is that same line. So the three points are collinear.

steps.slogan: Join the general case and the collinear-centers case.
steps.detail: The two cases cover every position of the three centers, and each gives collinear meeting points. So $E_{12}$, $E_{13}$ and $E_{23}$ are collinear.

concepts.c:circle: Each circle contributes its center and radius to the ratios.
concepts.c:tangent-line: The external tangent lines of a pair define the meeting point.
concepts.c:collinear-points: Collinearity of the three meeting points is the claim of the theorem.
concepts.c:homothety: The meeting point is the center of the homothety between two circles.

source.note: The classical proof by Menelaus' theorem, which the catalog lists as the prerequisite of Monge's theorem.

proofs.name: Lift to space
proofs.slogan: Lift each circle to a point in space, then see that the meeting points lie on the intersection of two planes.
proofs.scope: Different radii again make the external tangents meet. The proof covers lifted points that span a plane and lifted points on one line.

roles.why: Different radii place the lifted points at different heights and make the tangents meet.

steps.slogan: Locate the meeting point as the center of the positive homothety.
steps.detail: An external tangent meets the line $c_ic_j$ at a point $E$, because $r_i\ne r_j$. Similar right triangles, and the fact that $c_i,c_j$ lie on one side of the tangent, give $c_i-E=\frac{r_i}{r_j}(c_j-E)$. So $E=E_{ij}=\frac{r_ic_j-r_jc_i}{r_i-r_j}$ for both tangents; it is the center of the [homothety](c:homothety) that maps circle $i$ to circle $j$.

steps.slogan: Lift each circle to the point $P_i=(c_i,r_i)$ in space.
steps.detail: Put the plane of the circles at height $0$. The line $P_iP_j$ meets the plane $z=0$ at the parameter $t=r_i/(r_i-r_j)$, and the point there is $\frac{r_ic_j-r_jc_i}{r_i-r_j}=E_{ij}$.

steps.slogan: Choose a plane through the three lifted points that is not horizontal.
steps.detail: The points $P_1,P_2,P_3$ lie in a plane $Q$; if they are collinear, take any plane through their line. The heights $r_i$ are not all equal, so $Q$ is not horizontal and $L=Q\cap\{z=0\}$ is a line.

steps.slogan: Show that each $E_{ij}$ lies on both $Q$ and the plane $z=0$.
steps.detail: The point $E_{ij}$ lies on the line $P_iP_j$, which lies in $Q$, and it lies in $z=0$. So $E_{12}$, $E_{13}$ and $E_{23}$ all lie on the line $L$, and they are [collinear](c:collinear-points).

concepts.c:circle: Each circle becomes one lifted point from its center and radius.
concepts.c:tangent-line: The external tangent lines of a pair define the meeting point.
concepts.c:collinear-points: The three meeting points lie on one line of two intersecting planes.
concepts.c:homothety: The meeting point is the center of the homothety between two circles.

source.note: A coordinate form of the three-dimensional argument, in which a plane meets the plane of the circles in the line of the three points.

statement: In any [triangle](c:triangle), the pairwise meeting points of the adjacent [angle trisectors](c:angle-trisector) are the vertices of an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle).

hypotheses.text: The figure $ABC$ is a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with angles $3\alpha$ at $A$, $3\beta$ at $B$ and $3\gamma$ at $C$.

conclusion: The points $P,Q,R$, where the trisectors nearer the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ meet, form an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle).

proofs.name: Trigonometric proof
proofs.slogan: Compute one side of the inner triangle from the law of sines and the law of cosines, and see that it is symmetric in the three angles.
proofs.scope: Each angle is trisected, so $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi/3$ and each of $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ lies in $(0,\pi/3)$. The sines below are therefore positive.

roles.why: The angles $3\alpha,3\beta,3\gamma$ sum to $\pi$, which gives $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi/3$ and the sides of the small triangles.

steps.slogan: Prove the identity $\sin3x=4\sin x\sin(\pi/3-x)\sin(\pi/3+x)$.
steps.detail: The rule $\sin(A-B)\sin(A+B)=\sin^2A-\sin^2B$ gives $\sin(\pi/3-x)\sin(\pi/3+x)=\tfrac34-\sin^2x$. So the right side equals $3\sin x-4\sin^3x$, which is $\sin3x$.

steps.slogan: Find $BP$ and $BR$ from the law of sines and the identity.
steps.detail: Let $\rho$ be the [circumradius](c:circumcircle) of $ABC$, so $BC=2\rho\sin3\alpha$ and $AB=2\rho\sin3\gamma$. The law of sines in triangles $PBC$ and $ABR$ gives $BP=BC\sin\gamma/\sin(\pi/3-\alpha)$ and $BR=AB\sin\alpha/\sin(\pi/3-\gamma)$. With the identity, $BP=K\sin(\pi/3+\alpha)$ and $BR=K\sin(\pi/3+\gamma)$, where $K=8\rho\sin\alpha\sin\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Apply the law of cosines in triangle $PBR$, where $\angle PBR=\beta$.
steps.detail: The two trisectors $BP$ and $BR$ of the angle $3\beta$ at $B$ enclose the angle $\beta$. So $PR^2=K^2\left[\sin^2x+\sin^2y-2\sin x\sin y\cos\beta\right]$, with $x=\pi/3+\alpha$ and $y=\pi/3+\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Read the bracket as $\sin^2\beta$ through a triangle with angles $x,y,\beta$.
steps.detail: Since $x+y+\beta=2\pi/3+(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\pi$, a triangle with these angles exists, with sides proportional to $\sin x,\sin y,\sin\beta$. Its law of cosines gives $\sin^2\beta=\sin^2x+\sin^2y-2\sin x\sin y\cos\beta$. So $PR=K\sin\beta=8\rho\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the computation at the other vertices and compare the sides.
steps.detail: The value $8\rho\sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma$ is symmetric in $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. The same computation at $C$ and $A$ gives $PQ$ and $QR$ with the same value. So $PQ=QR=PR$, and $PQR$ is equilateral.

concepts.c:triangle: The proof computes inside the triangle $ABC$ and its small triangles.
concepts.c:angle-trisector: The trisectors give the angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ of the small triangles.
concepts.c:equilateral-triangle: Three equal sides $PQ$, $QR$, $PR$ show that $PQR$ is equilateral.
concepts.c:circumcircle: The circumradius turns side lengths into sines of the angles.

source.note: The standard trigonometric proof: the law of sines for the lengths, the triple-angle identity, then the law of cosines.

statement: Let $S$ be a [Noetherian scheme](c:is-noetherian) and $f\colon X\to S$ a [separated](c:is-separated) [morphism of finite type](c:morphism-of-finite-type). Then $f$ factors as an [open immersion](c:is-open-immersion) $X\to\overline{X}$ followed by a [proper](c:proper-map) morphism $\overline{X}\to S$.

hypotheses.text: The base $S$ is a [Noetherian scheme](c:is-noetherian).
The morphism $f$ is [separated](c:is-separated).
The morphism $f$ is of [finite type](c:morphism-of-finite-type).

conclusion: There are an open immersion $j\colon X\to\overline{X}$ and a proper morphism $\overline{f}\colon\overline{X}\to S$ with $f=\overline{f}\circ j$.

proofs.name: Deligne's scheme-theoretic form of Nagata's proof
proofs.slogan: Compactify affine pieces in projective space, then glue the compactifications by Deligne's version of Nagata's argument.
proofs.scope: The proof is an outline that rests on the cited text for the gluing step. The cited text proves the theorem for quasi-compact and quasi-separated bases, which includes Noetherian $S$.

roles.why: A Noetherian base allows the reductions to simple special cases.
Finite type makes each affine piece a closed subscheme of an affine space over the base.
The conclusion forces $f$ to be separated, so the hypothesis cannot be dropped.

steps.slogan: Reduce the theorem to simpler special cases.
steps.detail: The cited text proves the theorem through a series of special cases, each more general than the last. The first reductions use approximation arguments and pass to simpler schemes, such as an integral $X$ over a base of finite presentation over $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Cover $X$ by affine open pieces and compactify each piece in projective space.
steps.detail: Each affine open piece $U$ of $X$ over an affine open of $S$ is a closed subscheme of an affine space over that open. Its closure in [projective space](c:projective-space) is proper over that open and contains $U$ as an open subscheme. These are the obvious compactifications of the pieces.

steps.slogan: Compare the compactifications of two overlapping pieces.
steps.detail: A compactification of one piece $U_1$ need not contain the points of a second piece $U_2$, so two such compactifications do not glue directly. Nagata handled this problem with valuation theory and Zariski-Riemann spaces.

steps.slogan: Glue the compactifications of the pieces into one compactification of $X$.
steps.detail: Deligne's notes, written up by Conrad, translate Nagata's method into the language of schemes. A delicate gluing process builds a compactification of $U_1\cup U_2$ from those of $U_1$ and $U_2$, and then of all of $X$.

steps.slogan: Check that the glued scheme is proper over $S$ and contains $X$ as an open subscheme.
steps.detail: The gluing gives a proper $S$-scheme $\overline{X}$ with an open immersion $j\colon X\to\overline{X}$ and $f=\overline{f}\circ j$. The hypothesis that $f$ is separated is necessary, since an open subscheme of a proper, hence separated, $S$-scheme is separated over $S$.

concepts.c:is-noetherian: A Noetherian base allows the approximation and reduction steps.
concepts.c:is-separated: A compactifiable morphism is separated, so the hypothesis is necessary.
concepts.c:morphism-of-finite-type: Finite type embeds each affine piece in an affine space over the base.
concepts.c:is-open-immersion: The open immersion $X\to\overline{X}$ is the first factor of the conclusion.
concepts.c:proper-map: The second factor is proper, so $\overline{X}$ is a genuine compactification.
concepts.c:projective-space: Closures in projective space give the obvious compactifications of the pieces.

source.ref: B. Conrad, Deligne's notes on Nagata compactifications, Journal of the Ramanujan Mathematical Society 22 (2007), no. 3, 205-257
source.note: Nagata's original proofs are in Imbedding of an abstract variety in a complete variety (1962) and A generalization of the imbedding problem (1963), both in J. Math. Kyoto Univ.

statement: Let $m\ge1$ and $mk\le n$. Then the representative map $\mathrm{val}$ is an $m$-[Freiman isomorphism](c:freiman-isomorphism) from the first $k$ [residues](c:modular-arithmetic) modulo $n+1$ onto $\{0,\dots,k-1\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$.

hypotheses.text: The number $m$ of summands is at least $1$.
The numbers $k$, $m$ and $n$ satisfy $mk\le n$.

conclusion: The map $\mathrm{val}$ is an $m$-[Freiman isomorphism](c:freiman-isomorphism) between the two initial segments.

proofs.name: Sums stay below the modulus
proofs.slogan: Sums of $m$ small numbers stay below the modulus, so equality of sums modulo $n+1$ is equality of integers.
proofs.scope: All $k\ge0$ with $mk\le n$; for $k=0$ both segments are empty. The argument needs only $m(k-1)\le n$.

roles.why: A sum has $m\ge1$ terms, and $m\ge1$ gives $k\le n$.
The bound $mk\le n$ keeps every sum of $m$ elements below $n+1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathrm{val}$ is a bijection between the two initial segments.
steps.detail: Since $m\ge1$ and $mk\le n$, we have $k\le n$, so $k<n+1$. Hence the [residues](c:modular-arithmetic) $0,\dots,k-1$ are distinct and each is its own representative. So $\mathrm{val}$ maps them onto $\{0,\dots,k-1\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum of any $m$ chosen elements below $n+1$.
steps.detail: Each chosen element is at most $k-1$. So the integer sum of $m$ of them is at most $m(k-1)\le mk\le n<n+1$.

steps.slogan: Compare a sum of residues with the sum of their representatives.
steps.detail: The residue class of the integer sum $\sum\mathrm{val}(s)$ modulo $n+1$ is the sum $\sum s$ computed in $\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)$. So equal integer sums give equal sums of residues.

steps.slogan: Join the bijection and the sum condition into an $m$-Freiman isomorphism.
steps.detail: For $m$-element multisets $s,t$ of the segment, both integer sums lie in $\{0,\dots,n\}$ by step 2. Two integers in that range are equal if and only if they are congruent modulo $n+1$, so $\sum\mathrm{val}(s)=\sum\mathrm{val}(t)$ if and only if $\sum s=\sum t$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)$. With the bijection, this is the definition of an $m$-[Freiman isomorphism](c:freiman-isomorphism).

concepts.c:freiman-isomorphism: The theorem says that val preserves equality of $m$-term sums in both directions.
concepts.c:modular-arithmetic: Sums of residues are computed modulo $n+1$ and compared with integer sums.

source.note: mathlib reduces Iio to Iic (Fin.isAddFreimanIso_Iic), bounds a sum of m values by m*k, and compares residues with CharP.natCast_injOn_Iio.

statement: For a rotation-invariant two-body interaction $V$, the coupled particle-hole elements are recoupled from the coupled particle-particle elements by [6j symbols](c:6j-symbol): $\langle ab^{-1}|V|cd^{-1}\rangle_J=\sum_{J'}(2J'+1)\begin{Bmatrix}j_a&j_b&J\\j_c&j_d&J'\end{Bmatrix}\langle ad|V|cb\rangle_{J'}$.

hypotheses.text: The interaction $V$ is rotation invariant, so $v(m_a,m_d;m_c,m_b)=\langle j_am_a,j_dm_d|V|j_cm_c,j_bm_b\rangle$ is an invariant tensor.

The particle-particle element couples $(a,d)$ and $(c,b)$ to $J'$, and the particle-hole element couples $(a,b^{-1})$ and $(c,d^{-1})$ to $J$, with [Clebsch-Gordan coefficients](c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient) and the hole phases $(-1)^{j+m'}$.

conclusion: The particle-hole element of angular momentum $J$ is the sum over $J'$ of $(2J'+1)$ times a [6j symbol](c:6j-symbol) times the particle-particle element of angular momentum $J'$.

proofs.name: Racah recoupling
proofs.slogan: Expand the invariant matrix element in the particle-particle basis and recouple the four angular momenta with a 6j symbol.
proofs.scope: The proof covers the recoupling identity for any rotation-invariant matrix element, antisymmetrized ones included. Nuclear texts add the fermion exchange sign when they apply it to the operator between particle-hole states, and this proof does not derive that sign.

roles.why: Invariance makes the tensor a combination of coupled pairs with one coefficient per $J'$.
The definitions of the coupled elements fix the sum that is recoupled.

steps.slogan: Expand the invariant tensor in the particle-particle coupling basis.
steps.detail: By rotation invariance, $v(m_a,m_d;m_c,m_b)=\sum_{J'}\langle ad|V|cb\rangle_{J'}\sum_{M'}\langle j_am_aj_dm_d|J'M'\rangle\langle j_cm_cj_bm_b|J'M'\rangle$. The orthonormality of the [Clebsch-Gordan coefficients](c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient) shows that the coefficient of $J'$ is the coupled element.

steps.slogan: Insert the expansion into the definition of the particle-hole element.
steps.detail: The particle-hole element is the coupled sum of $v(m_a,-m_d';m_c,-m_b')$ with the phases $(-1)^{j_b+m_b'+j_d+m_d'}$. After the insertion it equals $\sum_{J'}\langle ad|V|cb\rangle_{J'}\,S_{JJ'}$, where $S_{JJ'}$ is a sum of four Clebsch-Gordan coefficients over all magnetic numbers.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the four-coefficient sum as a recoupling coefficient.
steps.detail: The sum $S_{JJ'}$ is the overlap of two couplings of $j_a,j_b,j_c,j_d$ to total angular momentum zero, with the hole phases turning $j_b$ and $j_d$ into conjugate representations. By the definition of the [6j symbol](c:6j-symbol) as a recoupling coefficient, $S_{JJ'}=(2J'+1)\begin{Bmatrix}j_a&j_b&J\\j_c&j_d&J'\end{Bmatrix}$; this value was also checked in exact arithmetic for several shell sets.

steps.slogan: Read off the particle-hole element as a weighted sum of particle-particle elements.
steps.detail: Substituting the value of $S_{JJ'}$ into the sum of step 2 gives the sum over $J'$ of $(2J'+1)$ times the 6j symbol times the particle-particle element $\langle ad|V|cb\rangle_{J'}$.

concepts.c:6j-symbol: The 6j symbol is the recoupling coefficient between the two coupling schemes.
concepts.c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient: Clebsch-Gordan coefficients define the coupled elements and expand the invariant tensor.

source.note: Racah recoupling of the m-scheme matrix elements, after S. P. Pandya, Nucleon-hole interaction in jj coupling, Physical Review 103 (1956), 956; recoupling coefficients as in Edmonds, Angular Momentum in Quantum Mechanics, Chapter 6.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) with [Hilbert class field](c:hilbert-class-field) $H$. Every ideal of the ring of integers of $K$ becomes a [principal ideal](c:principal-ideal) of the ring of integers of $H$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), and $H$ is its [Hilbert class field](c:hilbert-class-field), the maximal abelian extension of $K$ unramified at every place.

conclusion: For every ideal $\mathfrak a$ of $\mathcal O_K$, the extended ideal $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_H$ is principal.

proofs.name: Artin reciprocity and the transfer
proofs.slogan: Turn the class groups into Galois groups, identify ideal extension with the transfer, and show that this transfer is trivial.
proofs.scope: The proof outlines the argument of Artin and Furtwängler and rests on the cited papers for the transfer identification and the group-theoretic theorem. Capitulation in other unramified extensions is not claimed.

roles.why: The Hilbert class field and its own Hilbert class field give the group $G$ with abelian $G'$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the second Hilbert class field and its Galois group.
steps.detail: Let $K_2$ be the Hilbert class field of $H$ and $G=\operatorname{Gal}(K_2/K)$. Since $H$ is the maximal abelian subextension of $K_2/K$, the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup) is $G'=\operatorname{Gal}(K_2/H)$. So $G/G'\cong\operatorname{Gal}(H/K)$ and $G'$ is abelian.

steps.slogan: Identify each class group with a Galois group by Artin reciprocity.
steps.detail: The [Artin map](c:artin-map) gives $\mathrm{Cl}(K)\cong\operatorname{Gal}(H/K)=G/G'$ and $\mathrm{Cl}(H)\cong\operatorname{Gal}(K_2/H)=G'$. Here $\mathrm{Cl}$ is the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group).

steps.slogan: Match the extension of ideals with the transfer of the group.
steps.detail: Artin shows that under these isomorphisms the map $\mathrm{Cl}(K)\to\mathrm{Cl}(H)$, $[\mathfrak a]\mapsto[\mathfrak a\mathcal O_H]$, is the [transfer](c:transfer) $V\colon G/G'\to G'$.

steps.slogan: Show that the transfer into the commutator subgroup is trivial.
steps.detail: Furtwängler proves that for a finite group $G$ with abelian commutator subgroup $G'$, the transfer $G/G'\to G'$ is the trivial map. This is the group-theoretic core of the theorem, and the cited paper contains its proof.

steps.slogan: Read off that every ideal class of $K$ becomes trivial in $H$.
steps.detail: The extension map $\mathrm{Cl}(K)\to\mathrm{Cl}(H)$ is the trivial map. So every ideal $\mathfrak a$ of $\mathcal O_K$ has $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_H$ in the trivial class, that is, $\mathfrak a\mathcal O_H$ is a [principal ideal](c:principal-ideal).

concepts.c:number-field: The theorem concerns the ideals of a number field.
concepts.c:hilbert-class-field: The ideals become principal in this field, which also gives the Galois group $G$.
concepts.c:principal-ideal: The conclusion says that each extended ideal is principal.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: The commutator subgroup of $G$ is the Galois group over $H$.
concepts.c:artin-map: The Artin map turns class groups into Galois groups.
concepts.c:ideal-class-group: Principality of an extended ideal means a trivial class in this group.
concepts.c:transfer: The transfer is the group-theoretic form of extending ideals.

source.ref: E. Artin, Idealklassen in Oberkörpern und allgemeines Reziprozitätsgesetz, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 7 (1929-30), 46-51; P. Furtwängler, Beweis des Hauptidealsatzes für Klassenkörper algebraischer Zahlkörper, ibid. 7 (1929-30), 14-36
source.note: Artin reduces the theorem to a statement about the transfer of a finite group, and Furtwängler proves that statement.
